subject: Chemistry
title: The Beirut Explosion of 2020
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Beirut Explosion of 2020.

hook.text: On August 4, 2020, 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate exploded in Beirut's port. The blast was felt 240 km away in Cyprus.

buildup.text: The ammonium nitrate had been stored unsafely in a warehouse for six years. Officials knew but did nothing.

discovery.text: A fire in a nearby fireworks storage reached the ammonium nitrate. The resulting explosion had the force of 1.1 kilotons of TNT.

twist.text: The blast created a visible shockwave and a mushroom cloud. It destroyed 6,000 buildings and left 300,000 people homeless.

climax.text: The explosion registered as a 3.3-magnitude earthquake. It remains one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded.

punchline.text: Six years of negligence, one spark. The same fertilizer, the same tragedy, 73 years apart.

quiz.question: Why did the Beirut explosion happen?
options: Improperly stored ammonium nitrate ignited after a fire in nearby fireworks
A military weapons depot was deliberately detonated
An earthquake ruptured underground gas lines

details.summary: In August 2020, approximately 2,750 tons of improperly stored ammonium nitrate detonated at Beirut's port, killing over 200 people, injuring thousands, and devastating much of the city. The chemical had been negligently stored for six years despite repeated warnings from port officials.
details.whyItMatters: Beirut showed that ammonium nitrate catastrophes continue despite a century of warnings. It exposed systemic governance failures and renewed global calls for stricter chemical storage laws.
takeaways: 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate sat in a warehouse for six years
The explosion was equivalent to roughly 1.1 kilotons of TNT
Multiple officials had warned about the storage risk before the blast

faq.question: How did 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate end up at Beirut's port?
faq.answer: The cargo ship Rhosus was detained in 2013 for unpaid fees and deemed unseaworthy. Its ammonium nitrate cargo was offloaded into a port warehouse. Despite repeated warnings from customs officials about the danger, no authority took action to remove or properly store the chemical.

faq.question: Could the Beirut explosion have been prevented?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Proper storage protocols, timely disposal, or sale of the ammonium nitrate would have eliminated the risk. At least six official requests to remove the material were ignored or blocked by bureaucratic inaction over the six years it remained in the warehouse.
